title: Palisade Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Palisade wells have a 31-foot median depth; typical completed-well costs run $7,600-$14,300.
h1: Palisade, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a house near Palisade means looking past the existence of a well permit. The local records show mostly shallow wells, strong reported yields, and a large share of monitoring wells rather than household wells. That makes the permit history useful, but it also means the averages do not automatically describe a future domestic well.

Within five miles of Palisade, Colorado, Mesa County records contain 245 permitted wells. Of those, 134 are recorded as constructed, 122 report total depth, four report pump yield, and seven report static water level. Use these figures to frame a site investigation, not to replace a driller's estimate, water-quality testing, or a review of the permit's allowed use.

sections.heading: Palisade well depths are usually shallow
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Palisade is 31 feet, and the middle half runs from 15 to 46 feet. Ninety percent of the wells with depth data are under 100 feet. The deepest record reaches 520 feet, so shallow ground is common but not guaranteed.

For a drilling bid, that 31-foot median is a useful starting point in the local alluvial and sedimentary ground. It is not a promise that a particular lot will produce water at that depth. The permit records also show 7% of wells between 100 and 300 feet and 2% between 300 and 600 feet. Local changes in gravel, clay, bedrock, and access can move the actual hole well beyond the neighborhood midpoint.

sections.heading: Reported Palisade yields are strong, but the sample is small
sections.html:
The reported yield median is 44.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 11.5 to 93.8 gallons per minute. Half of the reported wells fall in the 5-to-15-gallon-per-minute range, and half report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 5 gallons per minute.

Those results look favorable for a buyer, but only four wells report pump yield. The dataset is dominated by monitoring permits, which make up 65% of the use mix. A monitoring well's construction and purpose may not match a domestic well. Ask for the well test, permitted use, pump information, and sustained production before treating the local median as an available household supply.

sections.heading: The recorded water level is shallow, with no reliable trend
sections.html:
Seven wells report a static water level. Their median depth to water is 15 feet, and the middle half is 12 to 18 feet. That indicates shallow recorded water levels in the small group with measurements, which is consistent with the shallow well depths found around Palisade.

The records provided here do not establish a water-table trend. A seven-well water-level sample is not enough to show that groundwater is rising, falling, or stable over time. Do not read the increase in permits—from 6 in the 1970s to 62 in the 2010s—as a water-level trend. For a purchase, have the driller review nearby static levels, seasonal conditions, and the intended well location.

sections.heading: Permit activity reaches from the 1970s to 2024
sections.html:
Palisade's permit history is active across several decades. The records show 6 permits from the 1970s, 16 from the 1980s, 48 from the 1990s, 56 from the 2000s, 62 from the 2010s, and 25 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2024.

The most frequently named driller or permit party is Authorized (Pe, Pg), appearing on 48 records. Owner appears on 5, and Mccracken Well Drilling Inc (Mccracken, Alan E.) appears on 4. Because many records are monitoring wells and only 10% are domestic or household use, compare actual construction reports from nearby domestic wells rather than relying only on the most common name in the database.

sections.heading: A median-depth Palisade well costs about $7,600-$14,300 finished
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground around Palisade, the typical drilling rate is $50-$75 per foot. At the local median depth of 31 feet, the drilled hole itself is modeled at about $1,600-$2,300. That is only the drilling portion and should not be mistaken for the price of a working water system.

A finished well, including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $7,600-$14,300 at the median depth. A longer hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, water treatment, or connection work can change the bid. Get the scope in writing and confirm what is included before comparing prices.

sections.heading: Palisade buyers should check quality, yield, and site limits
sections.html:
Environmental review deserves attention. Within about 10 miles, the mapped information includes 28 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 25 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 13 historic mine features. These locations do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to test the water and review nearby land uses before closing.

Low yield and dry holes remain site-specific risks even though the reported yield figures are high. Confirm the DWR permit, permitted use, casing and grout, pump test, and static level. Also plan septic and building locations together. Setbacks, soil, access for drilling equipment, trenching, electrical service, and the required septic design can affect where a home and well can actually go.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Palisade, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Palisade is 31 feet. The middle half runs from 15 to 46 feet, and 90% are under 100 feet. However, the deepest record is 520 feet, so a shallow neighborhood average does not guarantee a shallow well on a specific parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Palisade?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50-$75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 31-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $1,600-$2,300. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $7,600-$14,300.

faq.q: How much water do Palisade wells produce?
faq.a: Only four wells in the records report pump yield, so the sample is limited. Those reports have a 44.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 11.5 to 93.8 gallons per minute. Half report 5-15 gallons per minute and half report more than 15 gallons per minute.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Palisade?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that any individual well is safe to drink. About 10 miles around Palisade, mapped information includes 28 PFAS sites, 25 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 13 historic mine features. Test the well for site-appropriate contaminants and routine drinking-water indicators before use.

faq.q: Are Palisade wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The available facts do not show a dependable water-level trend. Only seven wells report static water level, with a median depth to water of 15 feet and a middle half of 12-18 feet. Permit counts by decade show activity, not groundwater decline, so check nearby measurements and seasonal conditions for a specific lot.
